ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *h₂ews-ye-tider. Proto-Italic *auziō Latin hauriō Latin exhauriō Latin exhaustusder. English exhaust From Latin exhaustus, past participle of exhaurīre (“to draw out, drink up, empty, exhaust”), from ex (“out”) + haurīre (“to draw (especially water), drain”).

senses.d: To draw or let out wholly; to drain completely.
ex: The water was exhausted out of the well.
Moisture of the earth is exhausted by evaporation.

senses.d: To empty by drawing or letting out the contents.
ex: to exhaust a well
to exhaust a treasury

senses.d: To use up; to deplete, drain or expend wholly, or use until the supply comes to an end.
ex: My grandfather seemingly never exhausts his supply of bad jokes.
to exhaust one's resources

senses.d: To tire out; to wear out; to cause to be without any energy.
ex: The marathon exhausted me.

senses.d: To discuss thoroughly or completely.
ex: That subject has already been exhausted.

senses.d: To subject to the action of various solvents in order to remove all soluble substances or extractives.
ex: to exhaust a drug successively with water, alcohol, and ether

senses.d: To expel (as exhaust).
ex: Infections can be reduced further if outside air is exhausted after a single use, rather than re-circulated.

senses.d: To discharge or escape (as exhaust).
ex: Steam from both high pressure cylinders exhausts through the respective receiver pipes into cylinders.

senses.d: A system consisting of the parts of an engine through which burned gases or steam are discharged; see also exhaust system.
The steam let out of a cylinder after it has done its work there.
The dirty air let out of a room through a register or pipe provided for the purpose.
An exhaust pipe, especially on a motor vehicle.
Exhaust gas.
Exhausted; used up.
